item.title: Why relocating wild animals is rife with complications
item.description: The social dimensions of moving wildlife were considered much less consistently than biological ones
item.content:encoded:
Moving large animals around is a seductive idea in conservation. If there are plenty of animals in one place and too few in another, moving some between the two seems an obvious solution. Sometimes it is. But with animals as large, mobile and socially complicated as elephants and rhinos, the move itself can turn out to be the straightforward part.

This autumn, 12 rhinos are due to be moved from a well-established reserve in North West Province in South Africa to another protected area, in the Waterberg region, as part of efforts to establish and strengthen secure rhino populations. I am involved with the conservation work around the move, including research that will follow what happens after the rhinos arrive.

But there are lessons from past projects that we have to bear in mind. In 2022, 263 elephants were moved around 350km from Liwonde National Park in Malawi to another park in Malawi, Kasungu National Park. Decades of poaching had severely depleted Kasungu’s elephants, while successful protection in Liwonde had allowed its population to grow. With Malawi’s protected areas increasingly isolated from one another, moving elephants from a relatively dense population to a much larger park with relatively few elephants made good sense.

item.title: Why Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize for Literature: For her bold, inventive, breathtaking work
item.description: The distance between classical literature and contemporary life shrinks thoroughly and repeatedly across her work.
item.content:encoded:
Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. The 76-year-old Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the news broke. The Swedish Academy praised her “bold and inventive” oeuvre for its “playful dialogue with the classical tradition”, through which she has fashioned “new forms for contemporary literature”.

In books like her 1998 verse novel Autobiography of Red (which has sold nearly 100,000 copies in the United States), Wrong Norma (2024), her recent poetry collection, and her 1986 debut Eros the Bittersweet – a book-length essay about the god of love – she challenges formal conventions and moves across literary genres.

Carson’s own account of what language can do offers a sense of the possibilities such invention opens up:

“words can squirt sideways, mute and mad; you think they are tools, or toys, or tame, and all at once they burn all your clothes off and you’re standing there singed and ridiculous in the glare of the lightning.'“

‘The easiest difficult poet’

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson studied classics at the University of Toronto and went on to teach ancient Greek. Eros the Bittersweet grew out of her scholarly training.

The petition alleged that around 600 persons were detained on Saturday and another 300 on Sunday.

Protesters were not allowed to assemble near Shivaji Park on Sunday and were detained at Dadar railway station, Scroll reported. Some persons were allegedly detained merely for walking in the area.

It urged the court to declare the “indiscriminate” detention of peaceful protesters and pedestrians without “lawful individual justification” unconstitutional.

item.title: The economy is made of people: Lessons from the Economics Nobel for India
item.description: Macroeconomic outcomes cannot be fully understood without examining the individual decisions that produce them.
item.content:encoded:
What does a central bank’s interest-rate decision mean to a household struggling with food prices, a small business deciding whether to expand or a company weighing a new investment? These may seem like very different questions. Yet they lie at the heart of a single economic problem: how do the decisions of households and businesses shape the wider economy and how can public policy influence those decisions?

This question sits at the centre of the work recognised by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, awarded to Robert E Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. Their research helps explain why understanding an economy requires looking beyond aggregate indicators to the choices, expectations and constraints of the people and firms that make it function.

For India, this is more than a theoretical insight. The latest figures show retail inflation rising to 5.54% in September from 4.83% in August, while food inflation climbed to 7.74%. The burden is not evenly distributed: rural headline inflation reached 6.08%, compared with 4.88% in urban areas.

item.title: Centre postpones rollout of UPI payments fee above Rs 2,000 to after Diwali
item.description: While the charges were scheduled to take effect on October 15, the NPCI said its implementation was deferred ‘keeping in mind the festive season’.
item.content:encoded:
The 0.4% fee on Unified Payments Interface transactions above Rs 2,000 to merchants will be imposed after the Hindu festival of Diwali, which will be celebrated on November 8 this year, said the National Payments Corporation of India on Tuesday.

The corporation is an umbrella body of retail payments and settlement systems operating under the Reserve Bank of India.

On September 14 and September 15, the Ministry of Finance issued notifications stating that UPI payments to merchants valued above Rs 2,000 would attract a merchant discount rate of 0.4%.

A merchant discount rate is a fee charged to businesses by banks to cover the costs of processing transactions. The rate typically ranges from 1% to 3% of the transaction value for credit card payments and can be up to 0.9% for debit card transactions.

On September 28, the Union government said that the charges would take effect on October 15.

The National Payments Corporation of India said on Tuesday that the decision to defer the implementation of the charges was taken “keeping in mind the festive season”.

item.title: How Khemkaran’s flat fields and irrigation canals helped the Indian Army defend the Punjab plains
item.description: An excerpt from ‘1965: Holding The Line at Asal Uttar’, by Harash Vir Singh and Shiv Kunal Verma.
item.content:encoded:
The Khemkaran Sector lay in the southwestern part of the Bari Doab, the tract of land between the Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej rivers. To the south and east stood the Beas and the Sutlej. To the north ran the Grand Trunk Road. To the west lay the Ichhogil Canal. The international border ran a short distance to the west of the canal before turning towards the northeast. The entire stretch of ground had a gentle fall from the northeast towards the southwest. Every nala, distributary, and surface drain followed this natural slope, and over time these channels shaped both cultivation and movement across the countryside.

There were three principal canals in this area, all aligned broadly from the northeast to the southwest. These were the Upper Bari Doab Canal, the Kasur Branch, and the Sobraon Branch. Beyond the Sobraon Branch lay the Beas and the Sutlej. Together, these water bodies not only irrigated the land but also canalized movement and created corridors between embankments where wheels and tracks could travel with relative ease. The very orientation of these corridors favoured movement from the Pakistani side towards the northeast in the direction of the Grand Trunk axis.

The Karnataka High Court on Monday struck down provisions of a 2022 law that increased reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in educational institutes and state government jobs, ruling that the enhanced quotas breached the 50% ceiling, Bar and Bench reported

A division bench of Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice KS Hemalekha declared Section 3 and Section 4 of the Act as unconstitutional, The Indian Express reported.

The law increased reservations for Scheduled Caste communities to 17% from 15% and for Scheduled Tribe communities to 7% from 3%. With the 32% quota for Other Backward Classes unchanged, the reservations in the state had risen to 56% from 50%.

The Act received the governor’s assent in January 2023 during the previous Bharatiya Janata Party government in the state and was given retrospective effect from November 1, 2022, Bar and Bench reported.

item.title: How Bengali writer Saradindu Bandopadhyay used Tibet scholar Sarat Chandra Das’s work for his novel
item.description: An excerpt from ‘A Babu among the Lamas: Sarat Chandra Das and the Making of Tibet Studies in Colonial Bengal’, by Parjanya Sen.
item.content:encoded:
In the opening article in the very first volume of the Journal of the Buddhist Text Society of India, “Indian Pandits in Tibet,” Sarat Chandra Das reconstructs the lives of the Tantric Buddhist masters who were key agents behind the dissemination of Buddhism to Tibet from India. Das focuses specially on the figures from Bengal, such as Atiśa, Kamalaśīla and Śāntarakṣita. Das translated and compiled these lives from the fourteenth-century Tibetan chos ’byung (narrative about the emergence of the Dharma) by the Sakya master Butön Rinchen Drub/ Bu-ston-rin-chen-grub (1290-1364). The article in the JBTSI would be expanded by Das into a book Indian Pandits in the Land of Snow (1893), edited by his brother, Nobin Chandra, and brought out by the Baptist Mission Press later, in the same year.

This biography of Atiśa by Das, translated from Butön’s chos ’byung would be featured within a new regional history of Bengal by another prominent Bengali intellectual of the time, Rakhaldas Bandyopadhyay/Banerjee (1885-1930), Haraprasad Shastri’s student and intellectual successor. One of the foremost Indian archaeologists of his time, Banerjee would inaugurate the idea of a new national and regional history, the first initiative of its kind, through his two-volume Bāngalār Itihās/ History of Bengal (first volume published in 1914; second volume in 1917). item.title: When an ‘untouchable’ man was convicted for praying at a temple 101 years ago
item.description: The successful legal battle to defend C Murugesan laid the grounds for a broader anti-caste struggle and India’s constitutional protection from discrimination.
item.content:encoded:
On the morning of October 13, 1925, C Murugesan walked through the stone gateway of the Sri Padmavathi Ammavari Temple in Chitoor district in Madras Presidency. The temple, in the town of Tiruchanoor, sits around 5 km from the foothills of Tirupati. Local tradition maintains that no journey to worship Lord Venkateswara in the temple on top of the hill is complete without the pilgrim first seeking the blessings of his consort at the base.

Murugesan belonged to a community then classified as untouchable. On that day, he carried no political banners nor did he march with a crowd. His only intention was to offer a simple karpura harathi, lighting camphor before the deity.

But his pious act was met by a swift response from the temple authorities. Within hours, the police arrested him under Section 295 of the Indian Penal Code, which related to the “defilement of a place of worship” carried out with the “intent to insult the religion of any class of persons”.

item.title: Why weight lost by restricting calories doesn’t often stay off
item.description: For many, the feeling of constant hunger is the main reason they don’t continue with calorie-restricted diets.

In the last few years, there’s been a lot of interest in calorie-restricted diets for weight loss.

These can vary significantly, from intermittent fasting (where you restrict eating to a certain window of the day), alternate day fasting (where you consume limited or no calories on every other day) to the Fast 800 which promotes rapid weight loss by drastically reducing calories with the “Mediterranean diet”.

The basic idea might seem obvious: reduce how much you eat, and you’ll theoretically lose weight.

But are they healthy? And will you just put the weight back on if you stop?

What are calorie-restricted diets?

The amount of energy you need each day varies based on your age, sex, body composition, how physically active you are, and any background health considerations.

Calorie-restricted diets aim to reduce a person’s overall energy (calorie) intake. And in certain instances, when managed carefully by health-care teams, there is evidence for their benefits beyond weight loss, including as an intervention before surgery.

The general aim is to eat less than the body uses, causing the body to draw on its stored energy – fat. Over time, this imbalance, generally using more energy than you eat, can lead to weight loss.

item.title: Can smallpox return from 500-year-old virus fragments?
item.description: The variola virus material found in Chile consists only of damaged genetic fragments preserved for centuries.
item.content:encoded:
Smallpox is the only human infectious disease to have been eradicated worldwide. Researchers have now recovered fragments of ancient DNA belonging to variola virus, the virus that causes smallpox, from the naturally mummified remains of two Indigenous people buried in northern Chile.

For centuries, smallpox caused devastating epidemics. Its severe form, variola major, killed around 30% of those infected, although the rate varied between outbreaks and populations.

The first documented outbreak in the Americas occurred on the island of Hispaniola in 1518. During the 16th century, successive epidemics became a major contributor to the catastrophic loss of Indigenous life, amid the wider violence and disruption of European colonisation.

In 1967, the World Health Organization (WHO) launched an intensified eradication programme, combining vaccination with surveillance and containment. The last-known naturally acquired case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

Live variola virus is officially retained at two high-security WHO-designated laboratories for approved research. The material found in Chile consists only of damaged genetic fragments preserved for centuries.

item.title: Nobel economics prize awarded to Robert Hall, Michael Woodford for stabilisation models
item.description: Their models have ‘significantly improved our ability to implement’ effective economic stabilisation policy, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in economics was on Monday awarded to American economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for stabilisation models.

Hall and Woodford developed new macroeconomic models that have “significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy”, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.

A stabilisation policy is a set of macroeconomic measures that governments and central banks take to stabilise the business cycle, maintain employment levels and keep inflation under control.

Fiscal and monetary policy measures based on these models “can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs”, the academy said.

Hall and Woodford were awarded the prize for “demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy”, it added.

“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” said the academy. “This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.”

The two economists will equally share the prize amount of 12 million Swedish kronor, or Rs 11.4 crore.

The prize in economics was the last to be announced this year.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘India’s Green Transition’ by Nirvikar Singh in ‘The Indian Economy: Navigating a Global Turning Point’.

India’s per capita energy consumption is less than 40% of the world’s average, but its energy system relies heavily on coal for power generation, as well as for industrial production. Oil is most important for transport, and biomass is most important for residential heating and cooking. Excluding biomass, in 2019, India’s total primary energy supply (TPES) was 734 million tons of oil equivalent (Mtoe), with just over half of this being covered by domestic production. Total final consumption (TFC) was 410 Mtoe, with industry accounting for the largest share, 42%, followed by the residential sector and transport.

India’s pattern of electricity generation and energy use imply that policies to achieve net zero have to have two main foci. The first is greatly increasing the role of cleaner sources of electricity generation, and the second is electrification of industrial production. Most were caused by just five pathogens: Helicobacter pylori (4%), human papillomavirus, or HPV (4%), hepatitis B (2%), Epstein-Barr virus (1%) and hepatitis C (under 1%). The Women Farmers Certificates will open doors for lakhs of women who sow, tend, harvest and manage our agri-foods systems, as well as livestock, poultry and fisheries, but are often left out of the formal definition of a farmer. Maharashtra has shown political will and a clear sense of urgency in bringing women farmers’ needs into the spotlight and leading by example.

Feminisation of agriculture

We have been witnessing feminisation of agriculture for some time now. As men move to non-farm jobs, women have increasingly taken up the role of managing and maintaining the agricultural lands.

Without land titles, they also struggle to access critical resources such as credit, water, technology and extension services, reducing them to labourers in a sector they largely sustain.

Beyond Our Births, Antara Mukherjee’s debut novel, is an exploration of the location of identity. Its narrative – that of a child abandoned by her Bangladeshi Muslim parents, adopted by a West Bengali Hindu family, forced to leave when the family’s fortunes turn, accompanied back to Bangladesh by her parents, only to escape from them soon after – continually questions the validity of our identity markers: caste, class, religion, nationality, gender; and underlines their intersectionality in our daily lives.

But the novel is perhaps even more a meditation on love – of its undefined, inexplicable nature, and its borderless provenance: for neither bloodlines nor boundaries between nations, or that between the human and animal can contain it. As protesters all over India demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner and the restoration of every citizen’s voting rights, I offer this musical note of solidarity.

For generations, Faiz Ahmed Faiz’s Hum Dekhenge has been an integral part of protests, a metaphor for resistance, justice and democracy, and since 2019 it has seeped into our wider national consciousness. The gold standard for this song is without doubt the rendition by Iqbal Bano in her stirring protest against Zia-ul-Haq, and that is the basis of this piece.

Hum Dekhenge is not an activist’s chanting song, shrill in tonality, fast in tempo, with an un-decorative melody. It is simple, yet nuanced in its flow and melodic direction. Iqbal Bano’s rendition is unusually slow, embedded with filigree work and subtle movements that allow the song to unfold evocatively.

item.title: Lessons for the 21st century from Mary Shelley’s 1826 novel ‘The Last Man’
item.description: Set in the late 21st century, the novel is about a lethal contagion spread by human conflict that sweeps the world and seemingly leaves one sole human survivor.
item.content:encoded:
Even if you have never read it, you know the story of Mary Shelley’s second great work of political science fiction after Frankenstein. The Last Man, published in 1826 but set in the late 21st century, tells the tale of a lethal contagion spread by human conflict and war that sweeps the world and seemingly leaves one sole human survivor.

With wars and climate catastrophes hitting a world still reeling from 7 million deaths caused by Covid-19, Shelley’s pandemic novel has perhaps never felt so relevant.

And the book’s influence is widespread. The tropes and themes of The Last Man have shaped the genre of postapocalyptic fiction in the two centuries since its release. In Shelley’s Frankenstein and the many stories, films and TV shows it has inspired, the abandoned monster becomes a plague upon his creator.

In The Last Man and the countless books and movies on its themes that followed, a human-made epidemic becomes the mega-monster that threatens the extinction of humanity itself.

Some of the recent television series that explore these themes are The Last of Us, Midnight Mass, and Station Eleven. They follow classic films such as I Am Legend, 28 Days Later, and The Last Man on Earth.

Regardless of how many zombie-invasion or vampire-apocalypse movies you have seen, if you haven’t read The Last Man, I recommend you do. And if you have, perhaps read it again.

item.title: How the French convinced Indian workers to stay on in the Caribbean despite systemic abuse
item.description: After slavery was abolished, Indian workers became vital to Guadeloupe’s sugar economy. When their contracts ended, colonisers tried to make them stay.
item.content:encoded:
When the Nantes-Bordeaux steamship left Indian waters and set sail for the French Caribbean in November 1888, it carried 597 men, women and children from Calcutta, Pondicherry, and Karaikal, all hoping to escape poverty by working for a few years in Guadeloupe.

The voyage quickly turned into an ordeal. After the ship broke down near Cape Guardafui, the passengers were stranded aboard at the port of Aden for a month while repairs were carried out. During the delay, many suffered from scurvy, a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency. By the time the ship reached Guadeloupe, four infants, two women and one man had died on board. Two men, apparently frustrated by the ordeal, jumped overboard.

The difficulties they faced during the voyage, however, were only part of the story.

French colonisers in the Caribbean had begun recruiting Indian indentured workers from the Madras Presidency, Pondicherry, Karaikal and Calcutta to address severe labour shortages on sugar plantations after the abolition of slavery in 1848. Many of the workers aboard the Nantes-Bordeaux had already lived in places such as Guadeloupe and Martinique and had chosen to return to the Caribbean because life in India presented its own economic and social hardships.

item.title: Wave of protests shows that Indian democracy’s greatest strength is its ‘million mutinies’
item.description: Just as when VS Naipaul wrote those words, today’s upheavals will transform India.
item.content:encoded:
In 1990, when VS Naipaul published India: A Million Mutinies Now, he gave India a phrase that has acquired an almost prophetic resonance: “a country of a million little mutinies.”

He was not predicting a revolution. He was describing something more consequential – the awakening of the individual.

Naipaul had returned to a country that had changed dramatically since his earlier, far darker journeys through India. He saw people emerging from the inherited certainties of caste, class, family, religion, region and tradition, demanding that they be allowed to decide for themselves who they were and what their lives ought to mean.

Emergence from dominant political thoughts was part of this process. His most important insight was that freedom does not necessarily arrive looking orderly.

“Independence was worked for by people more or less at the top; the freedom it brought has worked its way down,” he wrote. And then came the crucial observation: “People everywhere have ideas now of who they are and what they owe themselves.”

That is the heart of Naipaul’s argument.

Freedom creates expectations. Expectations create demands. Demands create friction. And friction creates protest. item.description: The curbs announced ahead of Saturday’s protest in Delhi show how curtailing movement can be used as an instrument for governing dissent.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, blocking transport has been among the most recognisable tactics of protest politics in India.

Farmers frequently block highways, unions organise chakka jams, and rail roko agitations have a history stretching back to the freedom movement. The logic is straightforward: disrupting everyday circulation makes a political claim harder to ignore. But the inconvenience caused to ordinary travellers is precisely why such tactics have also attracted criticism.

The state, of course, has also restricted movement during protests for a long time. Roads have been barricaded, protest sites cordoned off, and access to cities curtailed in the name of public order. During the 2020-’21 farmers’ protests, Delhi’s borders were fortified by digging ditches, erecting concrete barriers, rolling out razor wire and even installing iron nails into roads.

The farmers were allowed to protest at the Tikri, Singhu, and Ghazipur borders, but their movement toward the institutions in the centre of the capital was constrained.

October 10 therefore is not the first time the state has deployed mobility restrictions. What is striking, though, is their sheer scale. item.title: At Pune’s MPSC protest, angry young aspirants say they have been betrayed by the state
item.description: A question paper leak has shattered the faith in what many believed was a trusted government recruitment exam.
item.content:encoded:
As 23-year-old Sakshi Ejgar prepared hard in Pune for the prestigious Maharashtra Public Service Commission exams, she felt growing anger as she studied “good governance”, one of her main subjects. “We learn about transparency, objectivity, social justice and aspire to become officers who work by these values,” said Ejgar. “But we are not even being allowed to reach that far.”

Since October 2, following a question paper leak in June and examination irregularities. thousands of state civil service aspirants have been joining a sit-in agitation near Pune’s SM Joshi bridge demanding justice. So far, 11 suspects have been arrested for leaking the paper for the drug inspector recruitment exam held in March.

Pune is a hub for thousands of aspirants like Ejgar, many of whom hail from farmer families in drought-prone parts of Maharashtra. They spend years studying for competitive exams in the hopes of landing a coveted government job. These students stay in small, rented accommodations and pay for access to study halls and libraries.

item.title: In Silicon Valley, AI companies are poaching talent from tech giants
item.description: Corporations like OpenAI and Anthropic are looking to build teams in countries like India and Singapore.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West.

Silicon Valley’s artificial intelligence talent wars are now playing out in Asia.

OpenAI and Anthropic are poaching top talent from US tech giants including Google, Microsoft, and Amazon to build teams in countries like India and Singapore to sell their products and strengthen engagement with policymakers.

Last month, Meta’s India and Southeast Asia vice president, Sandhya Devanathan, left the company after a decade to join OpenAI as vice president for Southeast Asia and Australia. This was at least the ninth hire by a US AI giant from an American big tech firm in Asia in the past year.

“The number of executives in India who’ve actually run a country-level P&L [profit and loss] for a global tech company, negotiated with Indian regulators, and built enterprise trust at scale is small, maybe a few hundred people across all of Big Tech India,” Arjun Jaggi, an applied AI researcher and executive adviser to Fortune 500 companies, told Rest of World.

item.title: Russia: ‘Plague’ death is causing panic but there is little reason to worry for now
item.description: The availability of treatment, rapid testing and contact tracing mean the outlook of plague is very different today.
item.content:encoded:
A laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, Russia, has died just days after falling ill with an undisclosed illness.

While reports of suspected plague have been circulating in the media, Russia’s consumer health watchdog has described the illness as pneumonia of unknown cause. The World Health Organization also stated the official cause of death has not yet been confirmed. Plague therefore remains only a possible explanation.

While this is a tragic death and an important investigation, it’s certainly not a reason to panic or sign that the Black Death has returned. The availability of treatment, rapid testing and contact tracing mean the outlook of plague is very different today.

Why is plague suspected?

It’s currently not clear what the laboratory technician’s cause of death was. But as the research institute where she worked studies plague bacteria, health authorities are right to consider plague as a potential cause of illness.

The illness that she experienced – a form of pneumonia that ended in her death just a few days of contracting it – also resembles symptoms of pneumonic plague.

item.title: Meta blocks viral video in post alleging that BJP candidate in Bengal bye-poll ‘looted votes’
item.description: There were widespread allegations of rigging and booth capturing by the Hindutva party during the election in Rejinagar on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday night, Meta took down a viral video that purported to show Bharatiya Janata Party candidate Shankharav Sarkar going behind the screen of a polling booth where an electronic voting machine was placed during the bye-election for West Bengal’s Rejinagar Assembly constituency on October 6.

The video, posted by Golam Nabi Azad, the BJP’s principal opponent in the seat, was removed in compliance with a legal request from Indian authorities, according to a message that Meta overlaid on the post. The Aam Janata Unnayan Party leader in his Facebook post had described the bye-poll as an “unprecedented farce in the name of democracy”.

He alleged, “The BJP candidate himself has looted votes!”

On Tuesday, Scroll reporters in Rejinagar witnessed the police turning away Muslim voters from some polling stations. Opposition workers alleged that they were intimidated in the lead-up to the vote and some independent journalists said that the social media pages through which they disseminated their videos had also been blocked.

When the results of the bye-election in Rejinagar were announced on Friday, Sarkar was declared the winner with 1,29,914 votes, while Azad received 54,098 votes. item.title: True Story: Why Gyanesh Kumar’s exit may not end the rigging of Indian elections
item.description: India’s election body has failed to check vote suppression in recent years.
item.content:encoded:
Delhi is under lockdown as the police have imposed unprecedented restrictions in the national capital to prevent young people from gathering at Jantar Mantar on October 10 to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The protests have been sparked by a recent report in the Indian Express that revealed that Kumar had kept his fellow election commissioners in the dark about crucial decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The exercise has disenfranchised millions of Indians.

But one resignation might not be enough to restore free and fair elections in the country since the problems with India’s election machinery run deep.

item.title: JNU sacks professor, a Congress MP, over sexual harassment allegations by students
item.description: Angomcha Bimol Akoijam had denied the allegations, stating that they had been made to tarnish his reputation.
item.content:encoded:
Jawaharlal Nehru University on Friday dismissed professor Angomcha Bimol Akoijam who had been accused of sexual harassment by 11 students, ANI reported.

Akoijam is a Congress Lok Sabha MP from Manipur.

The complaints of sexual harassment against Akoijam had been submitted to the university’s internal committee four months ago, The Times of India reported.

Akoijam, who lives on campus, has been accused of inviting students to his residence for gatherings and making sexual advances, the newspaper reported. Some complainants also alleged that he made allegedly lewd and inappropriate comments during classes and viva examinations, including demands for sexual acts in exchange for marks.

Akoijam had denied the allegations, accusing what he described as “racist schemers” attempting to tarnish his reputation with unverified claims and lies, India Today reported.

The university said on Friday that the allegations against Akoijam had been investigated by the internal committee. Based on the panel’s findings, the professor at the Centre for the Study of Social Systems was dismissed from service with immediate effect.

Responding to the development, Akoijam said he does not have the dismissal order, reported PTI.

“Poobi! E…i Poobi!” Sheetli called her from the back, giggling.

Poobi ran off, remnants of food still on her fingers.

She was dressed in a floppy, faded gown, the one she was eating in. Hardly an elaborate meal – merely two ladles of rice scraped off the bottom of the pot. Poobi was waiting with a few stray shrimps and a sea of curry on her plate, confident that her mother would give her all the rice. She was chewing the shrimp shells with great concentration. But Poobi’s mother Chinta gave Sheetli the entire portion of rice without a second thought; Sheetli’s plate was dry, without any curry on it. item.title: Brij Bhushan Singh gets time to respond to plea against his acquittal in sexual harassment case
item.description: The Delhi Police sought 15 days to decide if it will appeal against the order clearing the former Wrestling Federation of India chief.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi court on Friday granted former Wrestling Federation of India Chief Brij Bhushan Singh time to file his response to an appeal filed by four women wrestlers challenging his acquittal in a sexual harassment case, Live Law reported.

When the court asked the Delhi Police if it would challenge Singh’s acquittal, the public prosecutor said the decision was yet to be made and sought 15 days, reported PTI.

The court posted the matter for hearing next on October 28.

On August 3, Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Ashwini Panwar of Rouse Avenue Courts acquitted the former Bharatiya Janata Party MP and his co-accused Vinod Tomar, a former assistant secretary of the wrestling federation.

In his order, Panwar stated that the allegations against Singh were “false and fabricated” and seemed to be “politically motivated”.

Noting that the complaint against Singh was filed long after the alleged sexual harassment, the court had said that the wrestlers’ accusations appeared to be “rehearsed, well-practised and planted”, while also observing that the complainants had maintained “cordial relations” with Singh for years.

The judge had also pointed out that the complainants had maintained “cordial relations” with Singh for years and invited him to family functions.

item.title: ‘Does not advance shared ambitions’: MEA on US suspending IT firms from green card programme
item.description: New Delhi said that United States Vice President JD Vance’s remarks, describing foreign workers as ‘indentured servants’, was ‘unwarranted’.
item.content:encoded:
India on Friday said that the United States’ decision to suspend several information technology companies from the permanent labour certification programme goes against advancing the shared ambitions of the two countries.

Permanent labour certification is a process that employers must complete before filing petitions for most employment-based green cards. Under the programme, employers must establish that there are no qualified, willing and available US workers for a particular job.

Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft, Adobe and India-based information technology companies Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL are expected to be affected by the Donald Trump administration’s decision.

The Indian external affairs ministry said that the permanent labour certification programme is different from the H-1B visa programme, which allows companies in the US to temporarily employ foreign workers for special occupations.

The suspension of permanent labour certification applications does not affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the persons who hold the visa and their dependents, it said.

However, it said that there could be “some impact” on the Green Card process of eligible employees of the affected companies. A green card allows a foreign citizen to live and work permanently in the US.

item.title: Assam woman found dead near railway tracks after complaining of drunk men aboard train
item.description: While the railway police said they suspect she fell off the running train, her family alleged that she was murdered.
item.content:encoded:
A 20-year-old woman from Assam who had called her family to say that she was feeling unsafe aboard a train from Visakhapatnam to Guwahati was found dead beside a railway track in Srikakulam district of Andhra Pradesh on Wednesday, reported The Hindu.

While the railway police said they suspect Himashree Boro fell off the running train, her family alleged that she was murdered.

Boro, a college student from Guwahati, had travelled to Visakhapatnam for a dance competition. She boarded the Kanyakumari-Dibrugarh Vivek Express alone at around 12.15 am on Tuesday, reported The Times of India.

Soon after, she told a friend and family members that she was feeling uncomfortable in a coach full of “unruly, inebriated” men, reported The Indian Express.

She had reportedly also shared a video with her family from inside the train before her phone became unreachable around 3 am.

The family contacted the railway helpline and were told that Railway Protection Force personnel would check on Boro.

Boro’s body was found more than 24 hours later close to the railway tracks in Tekkali in Srikakulam, The Assam Tribune reported.

The police have registered a case under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita section relating to suspicious death.

Members of the B Barooah College Students’ Union held a protest on Thursday, demanding a thorough investigation into the circumstances leading to Boro’s death, The Assam Tribune reported.

item.title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay for promoting international law
item.description: Pillay, who is of Indian-Tamil origin, showed that legal measures can help prevent war and violence, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Peace Prize was on Friday awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Pillay, 85, was born into an Indian-origin Tamil family under apartheid in Durban. She has been “confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion”, said the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

Her commitment to universal legal principles and her “firm moral compass” are constants in a long career, the committee said. “A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” it added.

Pillay has “significantly enlarged the scope and impact” of international law, the panel said.

She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court.

Pillay was also the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. She is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide.
